overview: Binary Search is an efficient algorithm for finding a target value within a sorted array. Instead of checking every element one by one like Linear Search, it repeatedly cuts the search space in half by comparing the target to the middle element, discarding the half that cannot contain the target. This halving is what allows it to search an array of a million elements in about twenty comparisons instead of a million.
intuition: Think of looking up a word in a paper dictionary. You do not start from page one; you open somewhere near the middle, check whether your word comes before or after that page, and throw away the half you no longer need. You repeat this on the remaining half until you land on the word. Binary Search does exactly this with array indices instead of pages.
howItWorks: Set two pointers, low and high, to the first and last index of the array.
Calculate the middle index between low and high.
Compare the target value to the element at the middle index.
If they match, the search is done and the index is returned.
If the target is smaller, move high to mid - 1 (search the left half); if larger, move low to mid + 1 (search the right half).
Repeat until the target is found or low passes high, meaning the value is not in the array.
keyCharacteristic: Binary Search only works correctly on sorted data; that is the price it pays for its speed. Every comparison eliminates half of the remaining search space, which is what produces its O(log n) time complexity.

overviewFaq.question: Why does the array need to be sorted first?
overviewFaq.answer: The whole algorithm relies on being able to decide which half to discard based on a single comparison; that decision is only valid if every element to one side of the midpoint is guaranteed to be smaller (or larger) than the midpoint, which is exactly what sorted order guarantees.

overviewFaq.question: Why is the time complexity O(log n)?
overviewFaq.answer: Each comparison discards half of the remaining elements, so after k comparisons only n divided by 2 to the k elements remain. The search ends when this shrinks to 1, which happens after roughly log2(n) steps.

overviewFaq.question: What happens if the target is not in the array?
overviewFaq.answer: The low and high pointers keep narrowing until low exceeds high, at which point the loop ends without a match, and the algorithm reports that the value was not found (commonly by returning -1).

overviewFaq.question: What is the difference between iterative and recursive Binary Search?
overviewFaq.answer: They perform the same comparisons in the same order, but the iterative version uses a loop and O(1) space, while the recursive version calls itself on each half and uses O(log n) space for the call stack.

overviewFaq.question: What is a common bug when implementing Binary Search?
overviewFaq.answer: Computing mid as (low + high) / 2 can overflow for very large indices in some languages; a safer formula is low + (high - low) / 2. Off-by-one errors in updating low and high (forgetting the +1 or -1) are another frequent source of infinite loops.

overviewFaq.question: Can Binary Search be used on something other than arrays?
overviewFaq.answer: Yes; the same halving idea generalizes to any problem with a sorted, monotonic search space, such as finding a boundary in a sorted answer range (binary search on the answer), which is common in competitive programming.

complexity.note: The best case is when the target happens to be the middle element on the very first comparison. The worst case (target not present, or found only at the last step) still only needs about log2(n) comparisons, because every comparison halves the remaining search space regardless of the input.

pros: Extremely fast on large sorted datasets: O(log n) means doubling the array size adds only one more comparison.
Uses only O(1) extra space in its iterative form, since it just tracks two index pointers.
Simple to reason about and prove correct, since each step strictly shrinks the search space.
Forms the basis for many other efficient algorithms and techniques, such as finding insertion points or search boundaries.
cons: Requires the data to be sorted first, which costs O(n log n) if it is not already; that cost can outweigh the benefit for a single search.
Works poorly on data structures without efficient random access, such as linked lists, where finding the middle element is itself O(n).
Cannot be used directly on unsorted or frequently-changing data without re-sorting or maintaining sorted order on every update.
Only finds exact matches (or boundaries) efficiently; it offers no advantage for problems that need every occurrence of a value scanned.
whenToUse: Searching a large, already-sorted array or list for a specific value.
Finding the boundary between two regions in sorted data, such as the first element greater than a given value.
Repeated searches on the same static sorted dataset, where the one-time cost of sorting is amortized over many searches.
whenNotToUse: Data that is unsorted and only searched once; a single Linear Search is cheaper than sorting first.
Data structures without random access, like linked lists, where Linear Search or a different structure (e.g. a balanced tree) is more appropriate.
Data that changes frequently, where keeping it sorted for every insertion or deletion may cost more than the search savings.

applications.title: Searching in databases and indexes
applications.description: Database indexes (B-trees) use the same halving principle as Binary Search to locate records in logarithmic time.

applications.title: Dictionary and phonebook-style lookups
applications.description: Any sorted reference lookup, from paper dictionaries to sorted in-memory tables, follows the same halve-and-discard logic.

applications.title: Finding boundaries and insertion points
applications.description: Used to find where a new element should be inserted to keep an array sorted (as in bisect / lower_bound functions).

applications.title: Binary search on the answer
applications.description: A common competitive-programming technique that applies Binary Search over a range of possible answers rather than array indices, when the underlying condition is monotonic.

applications.title: Version control bisecting
applications.description: Tools like git bisect use Binary Search to find the commit that introduced a bug by halving the range of commits each step.
